question:
There are \(5\) coins placed flat on a table according to the figure. What is the order of the coins from top to bottom?

[Figure 1](figures/2011_AMC_12A_Q02_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
When one coin's outline disappears behind another coin, the covering coin is above it. We must combine these comparisons without assigning an order to coins that do not overlap.

The displayed overlaps show that \(C\) is above \(A,D,E\), that \(E\) is above \(D\), and that both \(A\) and \(D\) are above \(B\). These comparisons put \(C\) above every other coin and \(B\) below every other coin.

The uncertainty is among \(A,D,E\). Coin \(A\) overlaps neither \(D\) nor \(E\), so the drawing does not determine its position relative to them. The only required order among these three coins is that \(E\) precedes \(D\).

Keeping \(E\) before \(D\), we can place \(A\) before both, between them, or after both. This gives all three compatible top-to-bottom orders:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(C,A,E,D,B),\\
&(C,E,A,D,B),\\
&(C,E,D,A,B).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are choices \(\text{A},\text{D},\text{E}\), respectively. The three possible positions of \(A\) exhaust the possibilities, and each resulting order preserves every visible overlap. Therefore the displayed figure does not determine a unique answer. The supplied choice \(\text{E}\) is one possibility.

answerCheck.adjudication: Root inspected the exact displayed clipping and stem, checked the nonintersecting A-D and A-E pairs, and independently enumerated the three compatible total orders A,D,E. Preserve source key E as historical; withhold ordinary automatic grading.
answerCheck.reason: The actual bound SVG contains real clipping, contradicting the first-pass claim that every outline remains complete. The visible intersecting pairs give C>A, C>D, C>E, E>D, A>B and D>B. In the common untransformed SVG coordinates, A has center (60.8217,31.7999), radius 31.298; D has center (56.5538,109.476), radius 40.6874; E has center (104.923,118.581), radius 40.6876. Their center distances are about77.79 for A-D and 97.35 for A-E, both exceeding the respective radius sums about71.99. Thus A overlaps neither D nor E, so the image cannot order those pairs. The three total orders (C,A,E,D,B), (C,E,A,D,B), and (C,E,D,A,B) all satisfy every visible occlusion. They are choices A,D,E. The source E agrees with its SVG paint order, but that hidden paint order is not uniquely recoverable from the displayed overlap constraints. Preserve the identifiable finite-order objective and propose source ambiguity, rather than invent an occlusion procedure or call the geometry entirely cue-free.
